steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on Guess & Sketch, a neurosymbolic method for assembly-to-assembly transpilation that combines a language model with a symbolic solver. Explain the need for cross-ISA software support, why neural and symbolic methods each fall short on their own, how the method works, and summarize the evaluation and headline results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Need for cross-ISA software support; limits of emulation and of current transpilers
- Why neural ML is a natural fit for transpilation
- Weakness of language models: long-tail logical reasoning
- Neurosymbolic approach
- Guess & Sketch method
- Evaluation setup and results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Cross-ISA need
  - heterogeneous hardware architectures + ISAs -> growing need for cross-ISA software management
  - hardware-specific legacy software must be re-written for other hardware
  - high-usage source files contain in-lined assembly -> needs porting
  - automated cross-ISA support: interest in architecture community for decades (cite)
  - emulators, VMs, containerized apps: simulate target architecture; unwieldy, compute-inefficient
  - assembly-to-assembly transpilation (cite): port from one ISA to another, natively executable
  - current transpilers engineered for specific source/target; scale poorly with new ISAs
- Neural fit
  - training pairs by cross-compiling C/C++ with different compilers and flags -> vast data
  - same semantics (same high-level program)
  - assembly syntax rigid but simple vs natural language / high-level PLs; LMs do well in such settings (cite)
  - automatic evaluation: compare execution of input and output code
- LM weakness
  - can't do long-tail logical reasoning (cite)
  - transpilation needs reasoning about complex program semantics
  - e.g. differing implementations of math operations across ISAs: critical, frequent
- Neurosymbolic approach
  - symbolic: correctness guarantees, but only short programs before intractability; classical synthesis struggles past \sim 6 lines of assembly (cite)
  - purely neural: powerful general translators, critical failure points -> program breakdown
  - mixed: LM obtains helpful info, passes to ISA semantics-aware solver
- Guess & Sketch
  - uses core LM properties to extract symbolic methods
  - Guess (neural): candidate translations, identify potential errors, extract semantically-aligned subsequences of input/output
  - Sketch (symbolic): potentially erroneous aligned subsequences; input subsequence = specification to correct output subsequence
- Evaluation
  - ARMv8 <-> RISC-V; generalizes to other source/target languages
  - new benchmark: 3 transpilation problems, varying difficulty and domain
  - engineered symbolic approaches have weaknesses; neural (fine-tuned, pre-trained off-the-shelf LLMs) struggle
  - ours: 57.6% more than GPT-4, 39.6% more than engineered transpiler, 13.2% more than most competitive baseline

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Hardware architectures and their instruction set architectures (ISAs) are more and more heterogeneous, and this creates a large and growing need for support for managing software across ISAs. This is especially relevant for legacy software that is specific to some hardware and that has to be re-written to run on any other hardware. Also, many source code files that are used a lot have in-lined assembly code in them, and this code has to be ported to other hardware architectures. The computer architecture community has been interested in automated cross-ISA software support for decades. Emulators, virtual machines and containerized applications let users run software on different host hardware, by simulating the architecture of the hardware platform the software was compiled for. But this option can be unwieldy and it is not compute-efficient. Assembly-to-assembly transpilation, which is the process of automatically porting software from one ISA to another, is a way to generate software that runs natively on the new hardware. However, the current transpilation tools are engineered for a specific source and target hardware architecture, so they do not scale well when new ISAs are introduced.

Neural machine learning techniques fit transpilation naturally. We can generate pairs of assembly program translations by cross-compiling C or C++ programs with different existing compilers and compiler flags, and this gives vast amounts of training data. The pairs have the same semantics because they come from the same high-level program. Assembly code syntax is rigid but it is simple compared to natural language and to most high-level programming languages, and existing language models have been shown to perform well in such settings. Evaluation can also be done automatically here, by comparing the execution of the input code and of the resulting code.

But a key weakness of language models in this setting is that they cannot do long-tail logical reasoning. Transpiling assembly code needs reasoning about the complex semantics of programs. Also, some specific challenging phenomena, like mathematical operations being implemented differently on different ISAs, are critical and come up often in assembly code.

- Neurosymbolic approach
  - symbolic: correctness guarantees, only short programs before intractability; classical synthesis struggles past \sim 6 lines of assembly
  - purely neural: powerful translators, critical failure points
  - mixed: LM gets helpful info -> ISA semantics-aware solver
- Guess & Sketch
  - Guess (neural): candidate translations, potential errors, semantically-aligned subsequences
  - Sketch (symbolic): input subsequence as specification to correct erroneous output subsequence
- Evaluation
  - ARMv8 <-> RISC-V; generalizes
  - new benchmark, 3 transpilation problems
  - symbolic weaknesses; neural approaches struggle
  - 57.6% more than GPT-4, 39.6% more than engineered transpiler, 13.2% more than most competitive baseline

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Hardware architectures and their instruction set architectures (ISAs) are more and more heterogeneous, and this creates a large and growing need for support for managing software across ISAs. This is especially relevant for legacy software that is specific to some hardware and that has to be re-written to run on any other hardware. Also, many source code files that are used a lot have in-lined assembly code in them, and this code has to be ported to other hardware architectures. The computer architecture community has been interested in automated cross-ISA software support for decades. Emulators, virtual machines and containerized applications let users run software on different host hardware, by simulating the architecture of the hardware platform the software was compiled for. But this option can be unwieldy and it is not compute-efficient. Assembly-to-assembly transpilation, which is the process of automatically porting software from one ISA to another, is a way to generate software that runs natively on the new hardware. However, the current transpilation tools are engineered for a specific source and target hardware architecture, so they do not scale well when new ISAs are introduced.

Neural machine learning techniques fit transpilation naturally. We can generate pairs of assembly program translations by cross-compiling C or C++ programs with different existing compilers and compiler flags, and this gives vast amounts of training data. The pairs have the same semantics because they come from the same high-level program. Assembly code syntax is rigid but it is simple compared to natural language and to most high-level programming languages, and existing language models have been shown to perform well in such settings. Evaluation can also be done automatically here, by comparing the execution of the input code and of the resulting code.

But a key weakness of language models in this setting is that they cannot do long-tail logical reasoning. Transpiling assembly code needs reasoning about the complex semantics of programs. Also, some specific challenging phenomena, like mathematical operations being implemented differently on different ISAs, are critical and come up often in assembly code.

Because logical reasoning in transpilation has symbolic properties, we propose a neurosymbolic method for transpilation. Purely symbolic methods are built on correctness guarantees, but generally they can only handle short programs before they run into computational intractability. Classical synthesis techniques have trouble scaling past \sim 6 lines of assembly code. Purely neural language modeling approaches are powerful general translators, but they have critical failure points that make the program break down. We argue that a mixed-method, i.e. neurosymbolic, approach is valuable: it uses probabilistic language models to get helpful information for transpilation, and then passes this information to a solver that is aware of ISA semantics to complete the transpilation.

Our method is called Guess & Sketch, and it uses core properties of the language model to extract symbolic methods for transpilation. In the neural Guess phase, a trained language model produces candidate translations for an input, identifies potential errors in the output, and extracts subsequences of the input and output sequences that are semantically aligned. The aligned subsequences that are potentially erroneous are passed to the symbolic Sketch phase, where the input subsequence is used as a specification for correcting the output subsequence.

We show that our method is feasible by porting assembly programs from ARMv8 to RISC-V and the other way around, but our method can generalize to various source and target languages. To test the method we introduce a new benchmark of 3 transpilation problems that vary in difficulty and domain. We find weaknesses in engineered symbolic approaches to the task. We also find that existing neural network approaches, with both fine-tuned and pre-trained off-the-shelf large language models, struggle with transpilation. Our method combines the strengths of the neural and the symbolic approaches, and it successfully transpiles 57.6% more examples than GPT-4, 39.6% more examples than an engineered transpiler, and 13.2% more examples than the most competitive baseline.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The increasingly heterogeneous landscape of hardware architectures and their instruction set architectures (ISAs) creates a large and growing need for cross-ISA software management. This challenge is especially relevant for hardware-specific legacy software, which must be re-written to run on any other hardware. Many high-usage source code files also contain in-lined assembly code that requires porting to alternate hardware architectures. Automated cross-ISA software support has been of interest in the computer architecture community for decades [1,2,3,4,5]. Emulators, virtual machines, and containerized applications let users run software on different host hardware by simulating the architecture of the hardware platform that the software is compiled for, but this option can be unwieldy and compute-inefficient. Assembly-to-assembly transpilation [6,7], the process of automatically porting software from one ISA to another, offers a way to generate software that can be executed natively on the new hardware. However, current transpilation tools are engineered for a specific source and target hardware architecture, so they scale poorly as new ISAs are introduced.

Neural machine learning techniques are a natural fit for transpilation. Assembly program translation pairs can be generated by cross-compiling C or C++ programs with different existing compilers and compiler flags, providing vast amounts of training data, and the pairs have the same semantics since they originate from the same high-level program. Assembly code syntax is rigid but simple compared to natural language and most high-level programming languages, settings in which existing language models have been shown to perform well [8,9,10,11,12]. Evaluation can also be done automatically, by comparing the execution of the input code and the resulting code.

However, a key weakness of language models in this setting is their inability to perform long-tail logical reasoning [13,14]. Assembly code transpilation requires reasoning about the complex semantics of programs, and specific challenging phenomena, such as differing implementations of mathematical operations on different ISAs, are critical and arise frequently in assembly code.

Motivated by the symbolic properties of logical reasoning in transpilation, we propose a neurosymbolic method. Purely symbolic methods are built on correctness guarantees, but generally can only handle short programs before running into computational intractability; classical synthesis techniques struggle to scale past \sim 6 lines of assembly code [15]. Purely neural language modeling approaches are powerful general translators, but have critical failure points that cause program breakdown. We argue for a mixed-method, i.e. neurosymbolic, approach that uses probabilistic language models to obtain helpful information for transpilation, then passes this information to an ISA semantics-aware solver to complete the transpilation process.

Our method, Guess & Sketch, uses core properties of the language model to extract symbolic methods for transpilation. In the neural Guess phase, a trained language model produces candidate translations for a given input, identifies potential errors in the output, and extracts semantically-aligned subsequences from the input and output sequences. Potentially erroneous aligned subsequences are then passed to the symbolic Sketch phase, where the input subsequence serves as a specification to correct the output subsequence.

We demonstrate the feasibility of our method by porting assembly programs from ARMv8 to RISC-V and vice versa, though our method can generalize to various source and target languages. To test it, we introduce a new benchmark of 3 transpilation problems varying in difficulty and domain. We identify weaknesses in engineered symbolic approaches to the task, and we find that existing neural network approaches, using both fine-tuned and pre-trained off-the-shelf large language models, struggle with transpilation. In contrast, our method combines the strengths of neural and symbolic approaches and successfully transpiles 57.6% more examples than GPT-4, 39.6% more examples than an engineered transpiler, and 13.2% more examples than the most competitive baseline.
